title: Optical imaging in dual-phase xenon time projection chambers for neutrinoless double beta decay searches
abstract: Dual-phase xenon time projection chambers (TPCs) are the leading technology for WIMP dark matter searches and have also demonstrated competitive sensitivities to neutrinoless double beta decays (0$νββ$) of \ce{^{136}Xe}. However, the large energy disparity between these two signals requires different detector optimizations. In particular, 0$νββ$\ searches in liquid xenon desire efficient rejection of closely located multiscatters of background gamma rays near the 0$νββ$\ energy, a capability achieved only in the vertical dimension in existing dual-phase xenon TPCs. We propose a highly customized, wide-angle optical system that can be conveniently integrated into large xenon TPCs and provide mm-scale transverse position resolution for MeV signals by imaging gas electroluminescence light. This approach preserves a TPC's low-energy sensitivity and optimizes a single experiment for both dark matter and 0$νββ$\ searches. This paper discusses the design, simulated performance, and implications of the imaging system for future liquid xenon-based 0$νββ$\ searches.

title: Ion Heating in Pair-loaded Relativistic Turbulence
abstract: Pair-loaded relativistic turbulence is expected in compact high-energy astrophysical environments and may sustain plasma heating. Using self-consistent three-dimensional radiative particle-in-cell simulations, we identify the mechanism of ion heating mediated by pair-enhanced radiative feedback in relativistic turbulence. We derive the theoretical criterion for the transition to a regime dominated by radiative feedback and show that pair loading promotes the growth and persistence of large, connected optically thick structures. These long-lived structures sustain intense localized ion heating, repeatedly generating prominent hot-ion clumps and substantially enhancing the mean ion temperature. Our results establish a physical link between pair creation and sustained ion heating, providing a theoretical basis for investigating intermittent hot-ion production in black-hole coronae and gamma-ray burst outflows.

title: Vacancy and Helium-Cluster Thermomigration in Tungsten
abstract: Strong thermal gradients in tungsten plasma-facing components can bias the migration of irradiation-induced defects and thereby alter their redistribution, interaction, and retention. Here, we extend an atomistic jump-statistics framework previously developed for hydrogen to quantify the thermomigration of a single vacancy and interstitial He$_1$--He$_4$ clusters in body-centered-cubic tungsten. Non-equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations performed over several thermal gradients are used to determine the directional jump ratio, while geometrically derived projected jump lengths convert the fitted directional-bias coefficient into the heat-of-transport coefficient $Q^*=αkT^2$, where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ the temperature, and $α$ a constant. All investigated defects exhibit negative values of $α$, corresponding to net migration toward the hot region. He$_4$ has the largest response, $α=-2.2457\times10^{-2}$ K$^{-1}$, followed closely by the vacancy, whereas He$_3$ exhibits the weakest response despite its intermediate cluster size. Independent constant-temperature simulations over 1000--1600 K show that He$_3$ is also the least mobile cluster and has the largest effective migration energy, $E_m^{\mathrm{eff}}=0.271$ eV. In contrast, He$_4$ is more mobile than He$_3$ and has the smallest effective migration energy, 0.087 eV. Agreement between the He$_3$ concentration profile predicted from the jump statistics and that obtained from a long molecular-dynamics trajectory provides an independent validation of the method. These results show that thermomigration cannot be inferred from cluster size, diffusivity, or migration energy alone and provide defect-specific heat-of-transport parameters for higher-length-scale models of tungsten under fusion-relevant thermal gradients.

title: Modeling and control of traveling wave structures with arbitrary beam loading
abstract: Traveling wave (TW) structures are widely used in linear or circular accelerators for beam acceleration. Unlike the standing wave cavities, the overall accelerating voltage cannot be measured by the probes installed in the TW structures. This creates difficulties measuring and regulating the accelerating voltage and phase felt by the beam when it passes through the structure. In this paper, a model of TW structures is developed, allowing us to estimate the accelerating voltage and phase from the measurement of the RF drive power input to the TW structure. The beam loading effects, i.e., the beam-induced accelerating voltage and phase in the TW structure, are also included in the model. With the TW structure model, control methods are proposed to stabilize the accelerating voltage and phase felt by the beam based on feedback, feedforward, and optimization. The validity of the TW structure model is confirmed with the test results at the SwissFEL with improved beam stability under the same RF feedback controller. This work provides a firm basis for developing the multiple-bunch operation strategy for SwissFEL required by the future upgrade with more beamlines.

title: Predictors of filament coil non-planarity in a dataset of QI stellarators
abstract: Stellarator magnetic fields are often realized with non-planar modular coils with their out-of-plane bending being one of the main engineering challenges. We ask whether the non planarity of the fialment can be predicted from the equilibrium alone. We look at a dataset of coils for stellarator equilibira and find that the geodesic torsion of the magnetic field line is a strong and robust predictor in a wide range of coil feasibility requirements. We compare the performance of the geodesic torsion against other equilibrium and surface geometry properties and find it to be a superior predictorv hardly replaceable by other quantities we considered in this dataset. The ranking it induces also reproduces the ordering of four published configurations --- precise QA, precise QI at nfp 2 and 3, and W7-X. Our conclusions suggest that geodesic torsion of the magnetic field line may be considered as a cheap and robust candidate for a stage-one non-planarity proxy.

title: An Algebra Bundle for Non-Composable Coincidence Probabilities in Gamma-ray Spectroscopy
abstract: Understanding nuclear level schemes from the detection of emitted gamma-rays is, at its core, a combinatorial problem. The transition matrix formalism that treats nuclear decay as a Markov process is a well established treatment for the prediction of emitted and detected gamma-rays. However, with the path algebra being the underlying algebra of such matrix methods, the formalism is restricted to calculating probabilities only for composable paths through the decay. This paper presents a new algebra that allows for the calculations of non-composable coincidence probabilities offering a more complete formalism for the prediction of gamma-ray spectra. The aim of this \textit{coincidence algebra} is to provide a general treatment for predicting all full energy summing peaks for composable and non-composable transitions. Non-composable summing peaks often corrupt peaks of interest by creating doublets in the energy spectra. The coincidence algebra serves as a tool for investigating any possible doublets produced from full energy coincidence summing. This formalism is tested for the prediction of gamma-ray peaks in the electron capture of $^{133}$Ba and compared to the results a Geant4 simulation of the decay within the GRIFFIN spectrometer. It is also shown how the path algebra formalism may be useful for understanding uncertainty propagation in nuclear level schemes.

title: Beyond Radiation Hydrodynamics: A Coupled Kinetic Plasma and Radiation Modeling of NIF Polar Direct Drive Capsule
abstract: Predictive modeling of inertial-confinement-fusion (ICF) implosions increasingly requires resolving ion-kinetic effects beyond the reach of radiation-hydrodynamics, without sacrificing radiation transport. We present, to our knowledge, the first coupling of a kinetic-ion plasma model to thermal radiation transport. The iFP code - a conservative, spherically symmetric, 1D2V hybrid kinetic-ion/fluid-electron Vlasov-Fokker-Planck solver - is extended with a grey P1 radiation model, coupled through a high-order/low-order (HOLO) fixed-point solver and advanced on a shared adaptive moving mesh. Opacities are mixed on the fly from the LANL TOPS library, exploiting the per-species information intrinsic to a kinetic code. We verify the implementation against the optically thick Marshak-wave and Mach-45 radiative-shock benchmarks, and apply it to a NIF polar-direct-drive exploding-pusher capsule. Increasing physics fidelity systematically improves agreement with the measured neutron yield and burn width; the improvement is driven by kinetically enhanced fuel leakage and ballistic preheating, and radiation transport proves essential for quantitative agreement. This work establishes a proof-of-principle capability for higher-fidelity kinetic-plasma/radiation modeling of ICF.

title: Optomechanical Detection of Individual Gas Collisions
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate the detection of momentum transfers from individual collisions of Kr, Xe, and SF$_6$ with an optically levitated nanoparticle, finding good agreement with theoretical expectations. The observed event rates accurately measure the gas partial pressures, while the spectral shape provides a sensitive probe of the surface properties of the nanoparticle, including its temperature. The reconstruction of impulse signals as small as 200 keV/$c$ further establishes that levitated optomechanical sensors can reach the sensitivity required for precision measurements of fundamental particle interactions, and demonstrates a proof-of-principle for a primary pressure sensor based on the detection of individual gas particle collisions.

title: Accounting for the detection response brings cavity ring-down spectroscopy to sub-permille accuracy
abstract: For nearly four decades, cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS) has been among the simplest, most widely used absorption techniques, requiring no calibration because it measures decay times, not intensities. Yet as accuracy requirements have tightened, CRDS has proven strikingly inconsistent: reported errors range from several percent to the permille level - the signature of an uncontrolled systematic effect so far worked around rather than resolved. This has confined applications demanding the highest accuracy - from testing ab initio theory to atmospheric sensing and quantum-based metrology - to a handful of laboratories relying on advanced calibration or architectures, at the cost of simplicity. Here we show the main source was hiding in plain sight: the detection chain's transient response. It distorts every ring-down, biasing the retrieved decay times differently from instrument to instrument - a bias that routine truncation of the early decay masks rather than removes. We measure this response with a calibration-free beat-note method and build it into the ring-down model. Validation uses a well-characterized carbon monoxide transition and an independent frequency-based reference. Across four detection configurations, line-intensity biases of up to 14 % shrink 41- to 87-fold, the results converge, reaching up to sub-permille agreement with the reference. This holds down to 4 us ring-down times, extending accurate CRDS to stronger absorption. Independent of the absorbing species and requiring no change to the CRDS setup, the approach turns a technique valued for its simplicity into one equally valued for its accuracy. Benchmark-quality measurement thus comes within reach of any CRDS laboratory.

title: Thermal Decoherence and Population Transfer of MeV Channeling Electrons in Diamond
abstract: Channeling radiation from MeV-regime electrons is governed by transitions between quantized transverse bound states, but experimental spectra are strongly modified by thermal diffuse scattering. To capture these open-system dynamics, a frozen-phonon multislice framework is combined with bound-state projection analysis to construct depth-dependent reduced density matrices in selected transverse manifolds. Beyond reproducing experimental channeling-radiation transition energies, this approach separates thermal population transfer, intra-manifold decoherence, and cross-manifold coherence loss. Applied to 16.9 MeV axial electron channeling in $\langle100\rangle$ diamond, the results show approximately exponential population decay from the initially occupied states, accompanied by strongly channel-dependent feeding among low-lying manifolds. Starting from a coherent superposition within the degenerate 2p manifold, stochastic symmetry breaking by thermal displacements drives the intra-manifold purity toward the maximally mixed limit, indicating rapid phase scrambling. Under 1s initialization, population transferred into the 2p and 3d manifolds remains internally close to maximally mixed, yet a weak residual 2p-3d cross-manifold coherence persists. This framework goes beyond static mean-field thermal broadening and provides a microscopic basis for evaluating population dynamics and coherence lifetimes in strongly quantized channeling-radiation systems.

title: Quantization Effects of Artificial Neural Networks for Embedded Edge-Computing Applications
abstract: This paper examines the use of Quantized Neural Networks (QNNs) for two resource-constrained scientific applications: automated calibration of semiconductor quantum bits (qubits) and scientific particle detectors. We evaluate the trade-offs between Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), and ultra-low-bit Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) with respect to latency and resource usage. Our results demonstrate that PTQ and QAT are easily implementable solutions achieving a four-fold reduction in memory usage for Ushaped CNN (U-Net) architectures, whereas BNNs are better suitable for use cases with challenging latency requirements. For the training of non-differentiable custom BNNs, we propose a novel, hardware-constrained learning approach using Genetic Algorithms (GAs). We showcase a Look-Up Table (LUT)-based BNN architecture suitable for direct conversion to Very High-Speed Integrated Circuit Hardware Description Language (VHDL) via the HCL4BNN framework. This method achieves nanosecond-scale inference latencies at 10 ns to 15 ns without requiring specialized Digital Signal Processor (DSP) or Block RAM (BRAM) resources.

title: Characterization of the R14374-10 photomultiplier tube for the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment
abstract: The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) is a planned cubic-kilometer-scale neutrino telescope that will be deployed in the Pacific Ocean, leveraging deep-sea infrastructure operated by Ocean Networks Canada (ONC). The first detector line will deploy 320 3-inch Hamamatsu R14374-10 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to detect Cherenkov light produced by charged particles propagating through water, as well as light from calibration sources and optical backgrounds. This article presents the systematic characterization of all PMTs to be integrated into the first detector line prior to deployment, ensuring compliance with all detector acceptance criteria. All PMTs satisfy the specified performance criteria: the average transit-time spread (TTS) was measured to be $1.73\pm 0.15\,$ns, and the average charge resolution at a gain of \num{5e6} was $0.43\pm 0.03\,$pC; the average after-pulse rate was measured to be around 6$\,\%$. The integrated P-ONE data acquisition (DAQ) system was also tested and cross-validated against a laboratory digitization system. The second part of the paper presents an in-depth characterization of a subset of six PMTs, focusing on the key properties required for detector simulations, including linearity, after-pulse rate, quantum efficiency, and relative collection efficiency. PMT linearity was measured at a gain of \num{5e6} using the complete P-ONE readout electronics, and the response was found to remain linear for signals up to 150 photoelectrons. After-pulse contributions from $\text{Cs}^{+}$, $\text{He}^{+}$, and other ions were identified in the subset. The peak quantum efficiency was measured to be $27.0\pm0.7\,\%$ at 395\,nm. Using measurements of the relative detection efficiency, the collection efficiency was found to differ by a wavelength-independent offset of 10--15$\%$ across the measured wavelength range.

title: Correlated detection of electrons and ions emitted from laser-induced nanoplasmas in doped helium nanodroplets in the single-shot single-cluster regime
abstract: We present single-cluster single-shot correlated measurements of electron velocity-map images and ion time-of-flight traces from individual laser-induced nanoplasmas in xenon-doped helium nanodroplets. Simultaneous detection associates the ion composition, ion kinetic energies, and electron energies with the same nanoplasma event. The detected ion composition separates events into populations dominated by He+ mono-cations versus those dominated by He^{2+} di-cations, with markedly different ion energies and electron kinetic energies. The He+-dominated population correlates well with low electron kinetic energies (< 0.5 eV), whereas the distribution of maximum electron kinetic energies for the He^{2+}-dominated population shows a peak around 1 eV. Molecular dynamics simulations averaged over the focal volume suggest that local laser intensity contributes to this separation. These correlations provide single-event observables for classifying nanoplasmas and will support real-time shot-to-shot sorting in single-particle coherent diffractive imaging experiments.

title: Fundamental limit of intensity scaling for harmonic generation on plasma mirrors
abstract: Plasma mirrors have the potential to considerably boost the intensity of ultra-intense laser pulses through high-order harmonic generation, offering a promising route to the extreme fields required for probing the strong-field regime of quantum electrodynamics (SF-QED). This prospect relies on the favorable scaling of harmonic generation with increasing laser intensity, a longstanding assumption that has remained untested at extreme intensities. Combining the first measurements of Doppler harmonic generation approaching $10^{22}\,\mathrm{W/cm^2}$ with advanced particle-in-cell modeling, our study reveals fundamental limitations to this scaling. We notably observe a strong reduction of the harmonic yield as the laser intensity is increased, and show using simulations that this originates from the interaction of the sub-picosecond laser pedestal with the plasma mirror. This pedestal drives a rapid evolution of the plasma surface, through radiation-pressure compression and surface modulations, which progressively suppress harmonic generation. By extending our simulations up to intensities of $10^{23}\,\mathrm{W/cm^2}$, we show that this evolution accelerates strongly with increasing intensity, eventually leading to plasma mirror disruption on the timescale of the main laser pulse itself, making pulse duration, in addition to temporal contrast, a second key parameter for efficient harmonic generation. These results reveal the fundamental limits of the intensity scaling of harmonic generation from plasma mirrors and establish the conditions required to preserve efficient harmonic generation at extreme intensities, providing critical guidance for their use as intensity boosters toward the SF-QED regime.

title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

title: The RUBIK satellite payload concept: a 3D-segmented plastic scintillation-based particle tracking detector
abstract: We present the design concept and first experimental results of RUBIK, a three-dimensional resolving plastic scintillation detector developed as a scientific payload for the Research and Observation in Medium Earth Orbit satellite mission of the Institute of Space Systems of the University of Stuttgart. The name RUBIK is inspired by the Rubik's Cube, a familiar example of a three-dimensional segmented structure, reflecting the 5x5x5 modular arrangement of the sensitive volume. The sensitive volume consists of 125 PVT-based plastic scintillator unit cubes, each penetrated by two perpendicularly aligned wavelength-shifting fibres, which guide scintillation photons to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), providing 50 independent readout channels. Custom readout electronics, comprising two discriminator boards with per-channel programmable thresholds, an FPGA-based data-acquisition board, and a dedicated power and bias distribution board, have been developed exclusively from commercial off-the-shelf components. A single-layer prototype with ten readout channels was used for concept validation through SiPM bias voltage and temperature characterisation, and a time-over-threshold based amplitude reconstruction method was validated against radioactive source and cosmic ray measurements. First hit-pattern measurements with 220 MeV protons at a clinical proton therapy facility confirmed that spatially resolved hit clusters consistent with the expected beam geometry were observable in the single-layer readout, demonstrating the capability to resolve particle-induced signal patterns as a first step towards 3D track reconstruction in the full instrument.

title: Reinforcement Learning Controllers for Fusion Scenario Development
abstract: Scenario development, the design of the waveforms that take a tokamak discharge from breakdown to flat-top, is still an iterative, labour-intensive process. Every candidate scenario has to be simulated with a controller in the loop, and the classical shape and current controllers need low-level actuator references. So the process is iterative and includes a number of trial-and-error steps. We propose to replace the per-scenario controller tuning by a single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller trained once, in advance, against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is then specified only by the target waveforms of the physical quantities of interest (plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, x-point positions), and the controller produces the coil-current and fueling commands that realize them. We demonstrate the approach on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up: the controller takes over a small limited plasma, ramps the current and the density, grows the cross-section, forms two x-points and holds a double-null diverted configuration against sampled shape targets for the rest of a 1.2 s episode. The neural network controller is trained using TQC algorithm. On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in 11-dimensional target space, the controller forms the divertor in 86% of the cases, holds it for more than 0.5 s in 67% and reaches the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%, with flat-top tracking errors of a few kA in plasma current, $\sim 0.15\times10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in density, $\sim 2$ cm in position and $\sim 8$ cm in x-point location; the failures concentrate at the high-current density ($J$) region which is believed to be physically or from engineering perspective not feasible within ohmic mode.

title: Time performance of USTC-IME LGAD under synchrotron light source focused X-ray
abstract: The time performance of Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs), designed by the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) and fabricated by the Institute of Microelectronics of Chinese Academy of Sciences (IME), was characterized at the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The experiment was conducted at the BL16B1 beamline, which delivers a focused X-ray beam with a diameter of 500 \textmu\text{m}, a repetition period of 2 ns, and a photon energy of 10 keV. Using a fast oscilloscope, waveforms containing continuous signal pulses were recorded within a 50 ns time window. The LGAD under test successfully resolved the 2 ns period of the SSRF. To mitigate pile-up effects and extract pulse-by-pulse information from the acquired waveforms, a waveform-level global template fitting method was employed. The time resolution was then estimated using a combined profile likelihood approach, with a restricted maximum-likelihood (REML) correction accounting for the per-waveform degrees of freedom, yielding a value of 136.8 $\pm$ 0.15 (stat.) $\pm$ 11.9 (syst.) ps. The complete reconstruction and fitting chain was validated end-to-end using simulated waveforms in which the timing deviations of individual large pulses were drawn from Gaussian distributions with fixed standard deviations. The effect of random photon absorption depth on the time resolution of LGADs was studied through dedicated simulations.

title: Phonon-dominated thermal conductivity of a superconducting amorphous MoSi thin film
abstract: We use the differential 3ω method to directly measure the temperature dependent thermal conductivity for about 90 nm Mo0.78Si0.22 thin films. The measurements are performed in a closed-cycle cryostat to access the temperature range between 50 K and 300 K. The MoSi thin films are capped with Al2O3 and probed with a Pt wire. The results show that the thermal conductivity does not satisfy the Wiedemann-Franz law. This implies that thermal transport in MoSi is not dominated by electrons but by phonon-like excitations, contrary to what is assumed in many electro-thermal models of superconducting devices. We argue that this property might be related to the weak localization visible in the resistivity as a function of temperature curves of the superconductor.

title: Experimental verification of the PRIORA Monte Carlo code for proton radiography
abstract: PRIORA (Proton Radiography Ion-Optical Ray-tracing Analysis) is a fast Monte Carlo model for high-energy proton radiography. It combines fitted proton-matter interaction tables with energy-dependent transfer maps of arbitrary order and simulates approximately $10^6$ protons/s through a complete ion-optical system on an 8-core laptop. We verify it with GSI data obtained with the Ta_bench target: fifteen precision slits in a 2 mm Ta plate between symmetric PMMA staircases. A single experimental image provides the image scale, spatial resolution as a function of chromatic load, signed focus in both planes, effective angular acceptance and multiple-scattering contrast. With identical processing of experiment and simulation and no physics adjustment, PRIORA reproduces the data obtained with 2 and 4 GeV protons. At 2 GeV, PRIORA also recovers sub-percent quadrupole trims consistent with the control-system records and determines a target-plane spatial resolution of $115\pm6\,μ$m.

title: Weak solutions for weak turbulence models in electrostatic plasmas
abstract: The weak turbulence model, also known as the quasilinear theory in plasma physics, has been a cornerstone in modeling resonant particle-wave interactions in plasmas. Stemming from the Vlasov-Poisson/Maxwell system under the weak turbulence assumption, incorporating the random phase approximation and ergodicity, it takes the form of a integro-differential system, which describes the time dynamics of particle distribution and wave spectrum. The interaction between particles and waves can be treated as a stochastic process, whose transition probability bridges the momentum space and the spectral space. To our knowledge, there is no preceding rigorous analytical work for the quasilinear theory addressed in this manuscript. In this paper, we establish the existence of global weak solutions to the one-dimensional electrostatic quasilinear model for nonnegative, smooth, rapidly decaying initial particle distributions and nonnegative, smooth wave spectra compactly supported in a positive wave-number band. The construction uses the resonance condition to reduce the coupled system to a scalar degenerate parabolic equation, together with uniform estimates and strong convergence of the gradients of regularized approximations. When the initial wave spectrum is positive throughout a single band, we further characterize the equilibrium selected by this approximation procedure. The equilibrium uniquely minimizes a quadratic functional over a nonnegative cone and admits a geometric construction through the least concave majorant of a primitive determined by the initial data. The limiting particle distribution is non-increasing on the corresponding resonant interval and forms plateaus wherever the equilibrium auxiliary function is positive. A relative-entropy argument establishes long-time convergence to this equilibrium.

title: Reduced Molecular Plasma Kinetics with Non-Boltzmann Vibrational Distribution
abstract: Vibrational kinetics can strongly affect energy transfer, chemical kinetics, and discharge behavior in molecular plasmas, but resolving all internal states is often impractical for reactor-scale simulation. Compact, physics-based vibrational closures are particularly needed when complete state-to-state (StS) data are limited. Starting from a detailed $\mathrm{H}_2$ StS plasma-kinetics framework coupled to an electron-Boltzmann calculation, this work develops a reduced vibrational-kinetics formulation. The $\mathrm{H}_2$ vibrational ladder is reduced to two non-Boltzmann groups that evolve their population and internal energy. State-resolved reaction rates and associated energy-exchange terms are projected onto the groups for subsequent tabulation in reactor-scale plasma models. StS-informed samples of the reduced-model are propagated for pulsed RF $\mathrm{H}_2$ plasmas across a scan of pulse-averaged absorbed power and compared with the corresponding StS simulations. Predictions from the sampled models reproduce the bulk plasma response, including electron density, atomic-H density, and $\mathrm{H}_3^+$ density. Discrepancies in $\mathrm{H}^-$ production and the upper-energy-group vibrational temperature persist across the sampled reductions. This indicates a limitation of the present VDF reconstruction rather than the nominal parameter choice. Tail-sensitive processes therefore require a more accurate representation of the vibrational distribution.

title: A General Treatment of Coupled Cavity Resonators
abstract: Consider several cavity resonators whose resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields are known, and suppose that they are coupled through apertures. How can the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of the resulting coupled-cavity resonator be expressed in terms of the original resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields? This is a problem frequently encountered in radio-frequency systems for accelerators. One example is a multicell cavity used in high-energy electron accelerators. In this note, the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of such coupled cavities are examined as generally as possible, based only on Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions. Specifically, the response function of a cavity as viewed from its coupling ports, namely, its admittance matrix, is derived, and a formulation is developed to express the coupled resonant electromagnetic fields using this matrix. The resulting formulation shows that the coupled resonant modes can be described in terms of overlap integrals between the resonant modes of the cavities and the waveguide modes at the coupling apertures. It also shows that the coupled resonant frequencies are given by the zeros of the determinant of a matrix constructed from the admittance matrices. The results thus obtained are applied to simple systems to confirm the validity of the formulation. Numerical calculations based on this formulation are also carried out for periodic systems in an attempt to derive dispersion relations.

title: Construction of crystal-based light sources with LWFA electron beams
abstract: We discuss a possibility to construct a crystal-based light source (CLS) of gamma-rays using electron beams produce by Laser Wake Field Acceleration (LWFA). This state-of-the-art acceleration technique is capable of producing few-GeV, ultra-short (fs) electron beams. In the case studies presented, we demonstrate the feasibility of novel gamma-ray CLSs based on exposing single crystals to electron beams available at the ELI-ELBA. The results of rigorous numerical simulations are presented to characterise the radiation emitted emitted by 1 and 4 GeV electrons incident on a 200-micron-thick single silicon crystal along the (110) plane. The simulations were performed using the current divergence as well as a smaller value that is believed to be a realistic to achieve in the near future. We demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve a photon yield of $10^6-10^7$ photons/s in the photon energy range from 5 to 50 MeV. Looking further ahead, we also performed a similar analysis for a 4-GeV positron beam incident on much thicker targets, up to 2 mm oriented silicon crystal. In this case, the photon yield can be increased by an order of magnitude.

title: One Component Plasmas Frequency Moments from the ISF
abstract: Dynamic structural characteristics of classical one component plasmas (OCP) are an essential tool for understanding of strongly coupled plasmas through experiments and numerical simulations. Here, instead of the dynamic structure factor, we focus our attention on the intermediate scattering function (ISF). Theoretical results are compared to those of obtained by the method of molecular dynamics (MD).

title: SynradG4: A Geant4-Based Extension for Synchrotron Radiation Background Studies in the ePIC Detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will operate at high luminosity with multi-GeV, high-current electron beams, resulting in substantial synchrotron radiation (SR) emission in the electron storage ring (ESR). A detailed understanding of SR photon transport in the complex three-dimensional interaction region (IR) geometry is critical for estimating backgrounds in the ePIC detector and for developing effective shielding and masking strategies.   This paper presents SynradG4, an EIC-specific extension of Geant4 for fast photon tracking in vacuum based on established models of SR reflection and rough-surface scattering. SynradG4 integrates the specular and diffuse photon reflection models of Synrad+ into the Geant4 geometry and field framework, while disabling all bulk matter interactions to achieve high-statistics transport through the 50-m-long IR vacuum system. The absorbed photons are then passed to a second-stage DD4hep simulation, in which electromagnetic processes such as photoabsorption, Compton scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and fluorescence are enabled for their propagation through the beam pipe and detector materials.   SynradG4 is not intended to replace general SR simulation codes; rather, it complements them by providing the workflow and geometry integration capabilities needed for EIC-specific background studies. Benchmark tests show that SynradG4 reproduces Synrad+ to within about 1% for both specular and diffuse reflection, and that it agrees well with Synrad3D and with the native Geant4 X-ray reflection model for smooth surfaces. Using the full IR geometry and machine lattice, we present the first SR background estimates for the ePIC detector and evaluate the impact of potential SR masks.

title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
abstract: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.

title: A 4-20 GHz Superconducting 90deg Hybrid Using Capacitively Loaded Coupled Lines for 2SB Heterodyne Receivers
abstract: We report the design and cryogenic characterisation of a broadband superconducting 90deg intermediate-frequency (IF) hybrid covering 4 to 20 GHz for sideband-separating (2SB) heterodyne receivers. The hybrid is implemented in thin-film niobium using capacitively loaded edge coupled transmission lines, avoiding the air-bridge interconnections required in Lange-coupler layouts while retaining a compact superconducting implementation with low loss and good quadrature balance. Cryogenic measurements using Vector Network Analyser (VNA) show amplitude and phase imbalance better than 0.6 dB and 6deg, respectively, across the full band. When used in a 2SB receiver, this level of IF balance is consistent with the observed image-rejection performance in the 10-20 dB range, for the full receiver. The design supports the development of wide-instantaneous-bandwidth 2SB receivers for millimeter and submillimeter observatories, improving spectral grasp for broadband line surveys and high-redshift line searches.

title: Analysis of collisional and facility effects in a magnetic nozzle plasma expansion
abstract: An axisymmetric, quasineutral three-fluid model is proposed to study the plasma expansion in a magnetic nozzle under the presence of neutrals coming either from the plasma source or as an homogeneous background. As a difference with other models, electron cooling in the plume is achieved by treating the electron energy flux as mainly convective and without the need to postulate any anomalous resistivity. Solutions are presented for the electron high-magnetization limit, in which the electron main magnitudes can be integrated along magnetic lines. Ionization, elastic and charge-exchange collisions with neutrals do not change the main qualitative features of the plasma expansion, known from previous collisionless models. Ionization enhances the plasma flow in the nozzle, and leads to additional electron cooling, which decreases the electric potential fall along the nozzle. The efficiency of the nozzle is quantified in terms of the gain of magnetic thrust and the plume divergence angle. Two types of boundary conditions are discussed for the electron flow: local current ambipolarity conditions at the nozzle throat and global current-free conditions at the outer boundary (i.e., metallic vacuum chamber walls). These last ones are shown to be physically more reliable: they introduce the influence of the chamber walls on the plasma expansion by shaping the ambipolar electric field; they permit the extrapolation to undisturbed free space conditions; and they approximate better experimental trends with the background pressure.

title: Reconstruction of Unobserved Core Electron Density in Tokamak Plasmas with a Neural Operator Transport Surrogate and Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. However, in a reactor-relevant device, diagnostic port access is limited and the profile can be observed only partially. In the present work we reconstruct the density profile by inferring the coefficients of a physics-based one-dimensional particle transport equation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast differentiable forward model. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.

title: Micrometer-thin liquid sheets from single-jet impact on a sharp edge for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments
abstract: We present a simple and robust method for generating freely suspended liquid sheets by directing a single laminar liquid jet onto the sharp edge of an inclined plate. By optimizing liquid composition, impact geometry, and flow conditions, we identify a 60:40 ethylene-glycol-deionized-water volumetric mixture for stable sheet formation. The resulting sheets span 8 mm in height and 3 mm in width, with thicknesses from 1.1 to 4.8 micrometers measured by spatial and spectral interferometry. Operated in vacuum as continuously renewed plasma mirrors, these targets demonstrate stable performance from 0.5 to 10 kHz using 175-fs Yb:KGW laser pulses, reaching a maximum S-polarized reflectivity of 66.5% at an intensity of 4 x 10^14 W/cm^2. At higher intensities using 25-fs Ti:sapphire pulses at 1 kHz, maximum S-polarized reflectivity reaches 77% at 2 x 10^16 W/cm^2. The reflected beam exhibits high temporal stability, with angular pointing fluctuations of 18.19 +/- 0.53 microradians. Our results demonstrate a tunable, continuously renewed liquid-sheet target for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments.

title: Critical magnetic Reynolds number of the weakly-collisional turbulent dynamo in supersonic plasmas
abstract: Weakly-collisional plasmas are found in several turbulent astrophysical environments, such as the Intra-galaxy-cluster medium (ICM) and the solar wind, where magnetic fields can be amplified by the turbulent dynamo. The onset of dynamo action is determined by the critical magnetic Reynolds number, ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}$, above which turbulent motions amplify magnetic energy. Although ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}$ has been studied extensively in collisional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, its value in supersonic weakly-collisional plasmas remains unknown. Here we determine ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}$ using three-dimensional hybrid particle-in-cell (HPIC) simulations of solenoidally driven turbulence with a sonic Mach number $\approx 2$. We vary the magnetic Reynolds number over ${\rm Rm}\approx31$-$1000$ and consider two initial plasma magnetisations, characterised by initial Larmor ratios $r_{\rm Larmor, 0}/L_{\rm box}=1$ and $100$. We find that the magnetic energy grows exponentially at sufficiently large ${\rm Rm}$ and decays when magnetic diffusion dominates at low ${\rm Rm}$. By fitting the magnetic-energy growth rate as a function of ${\rm Rm}$, we measure ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}=190^{+21}_{-17}$ and $198^{+16}_{-18}$ for the initially magnetised and unmagnetised plasma, respectively. These values are the same within their uncertainties, indicating that the initial plasma magnetisation does not significantly affect ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}$ in the supersonic regime. The measured values are higher than those previously obtained for the subsonic weakly-collisional dynamo, showing that increasing compressibility makes weakly-collisional turbulent dynamo action more difficult to excite. The measured values are also approximately 1.5 times higher than the ${\rm Rm}_{\rm crit}$ value reported for supersonic MHD turbulence.

title: PRIMA prototype spaceflight KID readout electronics laboratory characterization
abstract: We present further development and testing of prototype kinetic inductance detector (KID) readout electronics for the PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA). PRIMA is a NASA Probe-class astrophysics mission concept with two science instruments, FIRESS and PRIMAger, which provide spectroscopic and polarimetric imaging from 24 to 261 um. Together these instruments will explore the far-infrared sky with spatial-spectral mapping speeds that exceed previous studies by orders of magnitude, opening a vast discovery space. This increase in mapping speed is achieved by densely packed ultra-sensitive KIDs and cryogenically cooled optics. The PRIMA flight readout electronics will use the build-to-print SpaceCube Mini v3.0 which houses a radiation-tolerant Kintex KU060 field programmable gate array (FPGA). A custom high-speed digitizer board is being designed along with an RF electronics (RFE) board. The RFE was designed to provide programmable gain, band filtering, and RF switching between instruments. The prototype readout electronics, including the RFE, use functionally equivalent parts to the flight parts. In this proceeding we measure the readout loopback noise performance in the second Nyquist zone and timestream cross-talk performance. We present preliminary sweeps with the prototype readout coupled to prototype FIRESS detectors. Lastly, we demonstrate a cosmic ray pulse detection and real-time removal with an algorithm implemented in firmware.

title: Development of microwave multiplexed readout for athermal phonon TES-based detectors
abstract: Continued advancements in sub-eV calorimetric measurements are being enabled through the athermal phonon detection channel, with applications spanning a diverse array of fields, including low-mass dark matter searches, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, and quantum information science. While Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) have achieved the lowest thresholds to date, they face significant scalability bottlenecks due to the inherent constraints of conventional SQUID readout architectures. To address this limitation, we present an update on R&D to develop practical, highly multiplexed, microwave readout for athermal phonon TESs, which can enable a dramatic increase in both sensor count and target mass, with a focus on sub-GeV dark matter searches as a target application. This work leverages advances from highly scaled mm-wave, x-ray, and gamma-ray TES systems, adapting them to the unique needs of low-threshold rare event measurements. We quantify the basic readout functionality and noise level in our dilution refrigerator testbed and demonstrate operation of a variety of TES devices with saturation powers significantly lower than mm-wave and x-ray devices. We demonstrate proof-of-concept multiplexed readout of background event pulses, bound the readout's contribution to the parasitic TES background load to <1 fW, and discuss a cryogenic inline RF filtering scheme. These results demonstrate practical solutions to several of the key challenges that must be solved before a next-generation athermal phonon detector at scale is realized.

title: Optical effects in Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs)
abstract: Optical time projection chambers (OTPCs) are well suited for applications that require the highest spatial resolution for particle track reconstruction. The MIGDAL experiment uses a glass GEM-based OTPC and observes a systematic excess in both the intensity and width of particle tracks in its optical readout, when compared with charge readout simulations. One hypothesis is that scintillation light produced inside a GEM hole during the avalanche propagates through the GEM substrate and exits neighboring holes. We present lab measurements testing this hypothesized optical broadening effect in three types of GEM substrates: glass, ceramic, and FR4. Our observations quantify this optical broadening and demonstrate it to be strongest in glass GEMs. Additionally, we use Geant4 simulations to both reproduce our observations and quantify optical broadening effects in realistic charge avalanches. Applying our glass GEM effects to simulated particle tracks yields increases of track intensity and widths by up to approximately 26% and 31%, respectively. This may explain the larger-than-expected track intensities and widths observed in the MIGDAL OTPC. This effect may be relevant to GEM-based OTPCs, with its magnitude depending on the GEM structure and detector-specific optical configuration.

title: Intermittent turbulence as the driver of stochastic heating in the near-Sun solar wind
abstract: Understanding the mechanism by which the energy is dissipated at small scales to heat the outer corona and expanding solar wind, is a primary goal of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission, and an outstanding question in heliophysics. Recent observational case studies have suggested that the dominant dissipation mechanism(s), stochastic heating (SH) or resonant heating (RH), may be modulated by the Alfvén `surface' ($M_A = 1$), while theoretical and simulation works predict that the mechanism should be modulated by the level of turbulence imbalance. We measure the local energy transfer (LET) rate from $9.8$ to $55$ solar radii from PSP observations, showing that the LET rate peaks at $M_A \sim 0.4 - 0.9$. We connect enhanced LET rates to signatures of intermittency, highlighting the key role that intermittent fluctuations play in heating the near-Sun solar wind. We compare the LET rate with estimates of the SH rate, finding that below $\sim 15$ solar radii the SH heating rate matches the LET rate provided intermittency is accounted for, regardless of $M_A$, while farther from the Sun, SH is unable to account for the observed LET rate. In contrast to predictions by recent theoretical works, this implies that `imbalanced' intermittent stochastic heating may be a viable mechanism to heat highly imbalanced, low-$β$ collisionless plasmas, and is likely an important mechanism of dissipation in the outer solar corona and near-Sun solar wind.

title: Polarization-dependent exchange effects in intrabeam scattering
abstract: The emittance growth due to intrabeam scattering (IBS) depends on the scattering cross section and is therefore affected by the exchange interaction of identical particles. However, as the IBS growth rates are typically dominated by small-angle scattering events and the exchange interaction only significantly alters the cross section at relatively large angles, the influence of the exchange interaction is usually small. In this paper, we calculate the small corrections to the growth rates resulting from the exchange interaction. We include the polarization dependence of the exchange term in the cross section, and so we also present the growth rates as a function of the beam polarization.

title: Time-over-threshold versus pulse-height energy reconstruction in a PbWO$_4$ calorimeter read out by SiPMs
abstract: The time over threshold (ToT) can be measured with a comparator and a time-to-digital converter, avoiding the waveform digitizers normally used to read out calorimeter prototypes. We assess how much the energy resolution degrades when the pulse height (PH) is replaced by the ToT, using data collected in June 2024 at the CERN PS T9 beam line with 2-6 GeV electrons on OREO, a calorimeter of two $3\times3$ matrices of PbWO$_4$ crystals read out by SiPMs and sampled at 500 MS/s, and 1-6 GeV electrons on a lead-glass calorimeter sampled at 100 MS/s. The ToT is emulated offline on the recorded waveforms and converted into an amplitude, so that the same reconstruction chain is applied to both estimators. For OREO in random orientation the PH gives $σ/μ$ = 3.6% at 2 GeV and 2.4% at 6 GeV. A single-threshold ToT worsens the resolution by 50-80%, because one threshold cannot cover the dynamic range, while a dual-threshold ToT gives 3.9% and 2.6%, i.e. 6-10% worse than the PH. Extending the waveforms beyond the 1 $μ$s acquisition window shows that the window is not the limiting factor, and an emulated shaper that reduces the decay time to 50-100 ns preserves the result with a ToT of 0.3-0.5 $μ$s instead of 1.2 $μ$s. The ToT-to-amplitude conversion can also be calibrated with a scan of the two thresholds, without any digitizer, with a resolution comparable to the one obtained with PH-based curves. For the lead glass, whose pulses are less than two samples wide at half maximum, the ToT cannot be emulated reliably. We also find that a previous analysis of the same data is consistent with a drift normalization that does not subtract the pedestals; subtracting them improves the resolution by up to 1.6 percentage points.

title: ModeCast: One-Shot Prediction of Linear MHD Eigenmodes and Growth Rates in Tokamaks
abstract: Large-scale magnetohydrodynamic instabilities break plasma confinement, can trigger disruptions, and constrain fusion reactor design; modeling a single configuration against them takes hours with a reference solver such as JOREK, and a design study requires thousands of hours. ModeCast is the first learned surrogate to return the complete linear stability assessment for MHD modes. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 45,000 JOREK simulations across thousands of equilibria, it screens stability across toroidal mode numbers n=1-4 and predicts the full spatial structure and growth rate of unstable modes. Excluding the equilibrium solve, inference on a single GPU is over 10,000x faster than multi-core JOREK linear stability runs. The gain comes from building the linear-phase physics into the formulation, objective, and inputs, yielding up to six times more training data. ModeCast misses none of the unstable held-out cases, and its predicted fields reproduce the simulation's measured physics, from magnetic island topology to resistivity trends. On a fixed-geometry resistivity scan outside its training distribution, refitting only the 22k-parameter growth rate head of the 145M-parameter network on four simulation halves the held-out internal kink growth rate error, and fine-tuning the whole network adds little. Because it is differentiable and returns full fields, ModeCast could in the future assimilate experimental measurements, providing a bridge to real devices and accelerating progress toward commercial fusion. Project page: zenithon.ai/research/modecast.

title: Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier
abstract: Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at $f_p - f_s$, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180$^{\circ}$ hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.

title: Eulerian ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid-Vlasov-Maxwell turbulence
abstract: In collisionless plasma turbulence, energy is transferred from electromagnetic fluctuations to the particles. However, the relative contributions of different ion energisation mechanisms remain unclear. We investigate ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid Vlasov--Maxwell simulations of decaying turbulence at $β_{i0}=0.25$ and $β_{i0}=4$, where $β_{i0}$ is the initial ratio of ion thermal to magnetic pressure. Using the exact ion momentum equation, we decompose the ion energisation rate $\mathbf{j}_i\mathbf{\cdot}\mathbf{E}$ into the work done on the parallel, diamagnetic, curvature, agyrotropic and polarisation ion currents. This decomposition requires neither gyrotropy nor scale separation and, therefore, remains valid where guiding-centre theory breaks down. We show that the agyrotropic term, which has no guiding-centre counterpart, accounts for $21\,\%$ of the energisation at $β_{i0}=0.25$ and $91\,\%$ at $β_{i0}=4$. We find that the dominant instantaneous energisation term changes with $β_{i0}$, from the polarisation current at low $β_{i0}$ to the diamagnetic and agyrotropic currents at high $β_{i0}$, at all resolved scales. In addition, we show that reversible exchange with the ion bulk flow dominates the instantaneous rate, so the time-integrated energy transfer is larger at $β_{i0}=4$ even though the instantaneous rate is smaller. Our results provide quantitative evidence that guiding-centre drifts alone cannot describe ion energisation in kinetic-scale turbulence and that the dominant energisation term depends on $β_i$. The results also highlight the key role of non-local thermodynamic-equilibrium effects in energy conversion in collisionless plasma turbulence.

title: Results from the GIF++ Long-Term Study of Eco-Friendly Gas Mixtures for RPCs
abstract: Gaseous detectors play a crucial role in high-energy physics experiments, yet their operation often relies on fluorinated gases with a very high Global Warming Potential (GWP). Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) operated in avalanche mode typically use high-performance gas mixtures based on high-GWP F-gases such as C$_2$H$_2$F$_4$ and SF$_6$. As environmental concerns grow and regulations become increasingly stringent, the development of sustainable gas mixtures has become a global priority. Within the RPC ECOGas@GIF++ Collaboration, a long-term R&D program has investigated eco-friendly gas mixtures for RPCs and assessed their performance under irradiation. RPCs operated with an HFO-1234ze/CO$_2$ mixture were exposed to high particle fluxes at CERN GIF++, accumulating $\mathcal{O}(10^2~\mathrm{mC/cm^2})$ over three years. This ageing campaign is now complete, and the detector performances have been systematically evaluated across a broad range of particle rates. This paper presents preliminary final results from the campaign, along with future perspectives.

title: Reconstruction of Magnetic Fields with a Physics-Informed Neural Network
abstract: Accurate reconstruction of magnetic fields and their gradients is essential for assessing and controlling systematic effects in precision measurement experiments. We have developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) method which reconstructs three-dimensional magnetic fields subject to the source-free Maxwell equations, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$. In an extension of our previous work on PINN methods for reconstruction of magnetic fields in inaccessible interior regions via measurements at exterior locations, we now demonstrate the feasibility of applying PINN methods to the extraction of magnetic field gradient terms from discrete measurement points subject to constraints from Maxwell's equations.

title: Macroscopic Stability of a Rapidly Rotating Isothermal Magnetic Mirror
abstract: The macroscopic ideal-MHD stability of an axisymmetric mirror device with sonic levels of plasma rotation is analyzed by approximating the plasma equilibrium as a rotating isothermal theta pinch possessing an artificial gravity. Starting from a set of single-fluid, ideal-MHD, isothermal fluid equations, a linear, second-order, eigenmode equation for the radial component of the Lagrangian fluid displacement is derived which governs the stability of the equilibrium to small perturbations in the case of an arbitrary plasma angular velocity profile. The stability of the m=1 and m=2 modes is investigated. For the case of rigid plasma rotation, the plasma is found to be stable to these two modes provided that it is sufficiently short in the axial direction. For the case of sheared plasma rotation, the $m=2$ mode is found to be difficult to stabilize. This is the case for both monotonically decreasing rotation profiles, and profiles that peak off the magnetic axis.

title: Conservative Numerical Construction of Vlasov-Maxwell Equilibria and an Exact Cancellation of $E\times B$ Flow by an Electrostatic Pressure-Gradient Flow
abstract: A class of Vlasov-Maxwell equilibria with pressure gradients is considered under symmetry assumptions that reduce the equilibrium equations to a nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations. Such equilibria provide self-consistent kinetic states with nonuniform thermodynamic profiles and potentially strong equilibrium electric fields, useful for fully kinetic stability studies of gradient-driven instabilities in the presence of equilibrium flows. The reduced equilibrium problem is posed as a nonlinear boundary-value problem for numerical solution, and a discretization is developed that preserves an associated energy invariant exactly at the discrete level. The resulting method provides a systematic means of computing nontrivial equilibria without relying on scale separation, and an alternative to constructing only approximately self-consistent initial states.   A key property of the species flows, identified within this model for any distribution function of the constants of motion, is an exact cancellation between the $E\times B$ flow and an electrostatically generated component of the pressure-gradient-driven flow. This follows directly from a structural property of the species force balance that arises from this type of symmetry reduction, and is verified numerically.   Additional numerical results demonstrate the conservative properties of the discretization. Representative equilibrium configurations, relevant to future kinetic instability studies, are also presented. An asymptotic approximation for the interior equilibrium, derived in the well-magnetized, quasi-neutral regime, provides an independent check on these results. The present setting is deliberately simple, providing a controlled framework for constructing and analyzing self-consistent kinetic equilibria and a starting point for extensions to more general symmetry-reduced configurations.

title: Proton-Number Fluctuations in $^{238}$U+$^{238}$U Collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 2.1$ GeV with the CEE Fast Simulation
abstract: The Cooling Storage Ring External-target Experiment (CEE) at the Heavy Ion Research Facility in Lanzhou (HIRFL) offers a unique opportunity to map the QCD phase diagram in the high-baryon-density region. In particular, higher-order cumulants ($C_r$) of event-by-event proton number distributions have been proposed as sensitive probes of the nuclear-matter phase structure. In this work, $^{\text{238}}$U+$^{\text{238}}$U collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 2.1$ GeV are generated using the JAM2 model and then processed through the CEE fast simulation with detector responses. Experimental analysis procedures, including centrality determination and particle identification, are also implemented. Proton-number cumulants up to fourth order and their ratios are calculated and compared with the true values. A track-by-track efficiency correction method is tested by introducing reconstruction efficiency within the TPC acceptance. An additional factor is also included to account for acceptance losses caused by the azimuthal gap between the two TPCs. Within the uncertainties of the current data sample, the corrected cumulants and cumulant ratios are consistent with their generator-level values. The event-sample dependence of the cumulant-ratio uncertainties is further investigated to estimate the statistics required for future measurements, revealing a substantial statistical cost associated with the acceptance compensation. These results provide a simulation-based assessment of the analysis feasibility and statistical requirements for proton-number fluctuation measurements at CEE.

title: Machine Learning on Heterogeneous, Edge, and Quantum Hardware for Particle Physics (ML-HEQUPP)
abstract: The next generation of particle physics experiments will face a new era of challenges in data acquisition, due to unprecedented data rates and volumes along with extreme environments and operational constraints. Harnessing this data for scientific discovery demands real-time inference and decision-making, intelligent data reduction, and efficient processing architectures beyond current capabilities. Crucial to the success of this experimental paradigm are several emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), silicon microelectronics, and the advent of quantum algorithms and processing. Their intersection includes areas of research such as low-power and low-latency devices for edge computing, heterogeneous accelerator systems, reconfigurable hardware, novel codesign and synthesis strategies, readout for cryogenic or high-radiation environments, and analog computing. This white paper presents a community-driven vision to identify and prioritize research and development opportunities in hardware-based ML systems and corresponding physics applications, contributing towards a successful transition to the new data frontier of fundamental science.

title: Towards Low-Energy Electron High-Resolution Spectroscopy with Transition-Edge Sensors
abstract: We present a study of the energy resolution of transition-edge sensors (TESs) for the detection of electrons in the 100~eV kinetic energy range. The TES is a Ti-Au bilayer with an active area of ($60 \times 60$) $μ$m$^2$ and a critical temperature of $\sim 80$~mK. The electron source is based on vertically-aligned multiwall carbon nanotubes located inside the cryostat, with electrons generated via field emission. For electrons in the $(92 - 99)$~eV kinetic energy range, we obtain a Gaussian energy resolution for fully-absorbed electrons of ($0.48 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.06$)~eV, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second systematic}. When considering the full-width at half-maximum of the peak \textcolor{black}{of the signal amplitude distribution}, the corresponding resolution is of ($1.4 \pm 0.2 \pm 0.3$)~eV. The former represents an improvement of $(47-60)\%$ with respect to previous results, and is mainly attributed to the reduction in the TES active area. The latter is instead an improvement of over a factor of 21, and is mainly due to the reduction in the emitting area of the electron source, which significantly suppresses electron back-scattering in proximity of the TES. These results represent a major milestone towards high-precision spectroscopy on low-energy electrons, which is a key objective for the PTOLEMY experiment.

title: Path-integrated electrostatic energization in laser-driven collisionless cylindrical convergence
abstract: Collisionless converging ion flows can sustain particle energization over an extended path, but the field channel responsible for the energy gain is not always identifiable. In laser-driven bladed microtube implosion, energetic carbon ions were previously observed alongside a self-generated gigagauss-class axial magnetic field [D. Pan and M. Murakami, Phys. Plasmas 32, 072107 (2025)], leaving the origin of their energization unresolved. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, field-particle power decomposition and trajectory-resolved work accounting show that radial electrostatic work accumulated along the converging path supplies more than 98% of the net in-plane electric work, whereas the azimuthal channel associated with the time-varying magnetic field remains subdominant. The peak local mean ion energy factorizes, to good approximation, into an incident-flow contribution controlled by laser intensity and a geometric enhancement that grows approximately linearly with the inner radius because ions accumulate electrostatic work over a longer convergence path. The path-averaged radial electric field $\langle E_r\rangle$ scales with the peak laser intensity $I_L$ as $\langle E_r\rangle \propto I_L^{0.47}$, favoring a geometry-pinned, comoving charge-separation structure over Debye-limited scaling. The peak local mean carbon-ion energy reaches 0.89 GeV. A smooth-cylinder control exhibits comparable peak energization, showing that blade modulation mainly affects poststagnation ion residence rather than the energy source.

title: A dry cryogenic platform with picometre stability for nanoscale and quantum technologies
abstract: Mechanically ultrastable environments within maintenance-free dry cryostats are needed for high-precision surface probe microscopy experiments, as well as next-generation quantum technologies. The most demanding applications require picometre-scale precision combined with multi-axis and millimetre-scale scanning range, while offering access to optical, microwave, and radiofrequency control and a vector magnetic field. We demonstrate a versatile platform for such systems based on passive and active vibration control for a commercial dry cryostat. Using a tunable optical microcavity as a sensor, we report vibration levels of 4.2 pm root mean square at 2.3 K over one hour without postselection. We further demonstrate drift-free long-term operation with stability below 8.6 pm RMS over 12 hours. Our system enables continuous and automated operation for next-generation high-throughput applications without the need for liquid helium infrastructure. Requiring only standard machining facilities and commercially available hardware, the design can be readily adapted for cryogenic optical, electrical and magnetic high-precision measurements across quantum science, surface science, and nanotechnology.
